listening.title: Riverside Sports Centre – Membership form
listening.intro: Em sẽ nghe một cuộc gọi điện giữa nhân viên trung tâm thể thao và một người muốn đăng ký làm hội viên.
listening.instruction: Điền vào phiếu. Mỗi chỗ trống viết KHÔNG QUÁ MỘT TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT CON SỐ.

script.text: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?
Hi. I'd like to join the gym. Can you tell me about the memberships?
Of course. We have two types. The standard membership is thirty-two pounds a month, and the student membership is twenty pounds a month.
I'm a student, so the student one, please.
Great. Can I have your full name?
Yes, it's Daniel Morton. That's M, O, R, T, O, N.
Thank you. And your date of birth?
The fourteenth of March, two thousand and five.
And what's your address?
Forty-seven Hill Road.
And a phone number?
It's oh seven seven one three, four five six, nine two eight.
Which university are you at, and what do you study?
Westfield University. I'm studying chemistry.
When would you like to start?
Next Tuesday. Actually, no. Thursday would be better.
Thursday is fine. We also run classes in yoga, swimming and boxing. Are you interested in any of them?
I used to do yoga, but I didn't really enjoy it. I'd like to try swimming.
Lovely. One more thing. Please bring a photo when you come, for your membership card.
A photo. No problem. Thanks for your help.

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the bicycle was seen as the transport of the poor. In many European cities, the number of people cycling to work fell steadily after 1950, as rising incomes allowed families to buy cars. City planners built wide roads and car parks, and cycle paths were often removed to make space for traffic.

This trend began to change in the 1970s. A sharp rise in oil prices in 1973 made driving more expensive, and some governments started to look for alternatives. In the Netherlands, public protests about the number of children killed in road accidents led to new policies that gave cyclists separate lanes and safer junctions. Today, more than a quarter of all journeys in the country are made by bicycle.

Other cities have followed more recently. Paris, for example, created hundreds of kilometres of new cycle lanes after 2020, and the number of cyclists on some main streets more than doubled within two years. Supporters argue that cycling reduces air pollution and noise, and that it is also good for public health, because regular cyclists tend to have lower rates of heart disease.

However, not everyone welcomes the change. Some shop owners worry that fewer car parking spaces will mean fewer customers, although several studies have found that people who walk or cycle to shops actually visit more often and spend more money over a month. Delivery companies also complain that narrower roads make their work slower.

Experts agree that building lanes alone is not enough. People are more likely to cycle when they feel safe, when there are secure places to leave their bicycles, and when they can combine cycling with trains or buses. In Tokyo, for instance, large bicycle car parks next to railway stations allow commuters to ride the first part of their journey and take the train for the rest. The future of urban cycling, therefore, may depend as much on good planning as on people's willingness to change their habits.

Oil prices rose more in the Netherlands in 1973 than in other countries.
In the Netherlands, protests about children's road safety helped to change transport policy.
In Paris, the number of cyclists on some main streets fell after 2020.
Studies show that shoppers who cycle spend less money each month than other shoppers.
Most delivery companies in Paris now use bicycles.
